summary: Introduces a generic mechanism in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol to group Label Switched Paths. Groups can express associations between sets of paths or between paths and sets of attributes, and apply to stateful PCE in active and passive modes and to stateless PCE.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8697 lets PCEP speakers group Label Switched Paths (LSPs) that are related. A shared association identifies the group so a PCE can apply common information or behavior to its members.

questions: what is the pcep association object
what is an lsp association group
what is an operator-configured association range
subtitle: Group related Label Switched Paths with a shared PCEP association object.

tldr.problem: Related Label Switched Paths need to share information for protection, reoptimization, diversity, or common policy, and separate mechanisms for each use would duplicate work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an ASSOCIATION object identified by type, ID, and source, plus OPEN-object TLVs for supported types and reserved ID ranges.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a common grouping mechanism; individual association types are defined elsewhere. RFC 8697 is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8697 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2020. The unit metadata says RFC 9756 updates it.

sections.title: Why Group LSPs
sections.content:
A stateful Path Computation Element (PCE) can update existing LSPs and create new ones. Several paths may need shared information, such as a working path and its protection path, an original path and its reoptimized replacement, or a set of diverse paths.

A stateless PCE can also associate a path computation request with a group so it uses common policy. Rather than define a separate grouping mechanism for each case, this RFC provides a generic one. It is distinct from the SVEC request-synchronization object in RFC 5440.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network paths need to be treated together, such as a working path and a protection path. This RFC defines one general way to identify those groups.

sections.title: Dynamic and Operator-Configured Groups
sections.content:
An LSP joins a group by being associated with other LSPs. Groups may contain paths from the same or different headends, and one LSP may belong to multiple groups of the same or different types.

A PCEP speaker can create a dynamic group and assign its parameters, or an operator can configure the group on the PCEP peers. The association is part of LSP state; a dynamic group exists while at least one LSP belongs to it. This RFC defines the group mechanism, not the meaning of each association type.
sections.plainLanguage: A path can belong to more than one group. A group is either created by a PCEP speaker or configured by an operator, and its type determines what it means.

sections.title: Advertising Supported Types and ID Ranges
sections.content:
The optional ASSOC-Type-List TLV appears in the PCEP OPEN object and lists the association types a speaker supports. It MUST NOT appear more than once in an OPEN object; repeated instances make the session invalid.

The optional OP-CONF-ASSOC-RANGE TLV advertises ID ranges reserved for operator-configured groups. Dynamic associations MUST NOT use IDs in those ranges. Invalid start IDs, zero ranges, overlapping ranges for one type, or a range that exceeds the largest ID cause session rejection.
sections.plainLanguage: During session setup, peers can list the association types they understand and the ID ranges reserved for operator configuration. Dynamic groups use other IDs to avoid conflicts.

sections.title: The ASSOCIATION Object
sections.content:
The ASSOCIATION object has Object-Class 40. Object-Type 1 carries an IPv4 Association Source, and Object-Type 2 carries an IPv6 source. The object contains flags, Association Type, Association ID, source address, and optional TLVs.

The R flag requests removal of an LSP from the association. The required Association Type, Association ID, and Association Source together identify the group. ID values 0 and 0xffff are reserved; 0xffff can identify all groups in the specified type and source scope when used with removal.
sections.plainLanguage: The object carries the group type, group ID, and source address. Its removal flag tells the peer to remove the LSP from that group.

sections.title: Using Associations in PCEP Messages
sections.content:
Stateful PCEP messages can report, update, or initiate LSP association membership. The first report for an LSP MUST include all its groups; later reports SHOULD include only changed or removed groups. A PCE-initiated LSP lists all groups when it is created.

A passive PCE may receive an association in a PCReq, or return one in a PCRep with NO-PATH to identify the group related to a failed computation. Dynamic associations are cleared with LSP state when the PCEP session ends. If an LSP moves to another PCE after a session failure, its associations remain unless the new PCE changes them.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP messages can add an LSP to groups, report its groups, or remove it. When a session ends, dynamic associations are cleared along with the related LSP state.

sections.title: Errors for Unsupported or Invalid Groups
sections.content:
A peer that does not recognize the ASSOCIATION object reports an unknown-object error. A peer that recognizes the object but not its association type returns Association Error value 1.

Other Association Error values identify conditions such as too many LSPs or groups, an unknown group, mismatched association information, failure to join a group, or an ID outside the configured range. Operators or local policy may set limits on group and LSP counts.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCEP peer reports why it cannot process an association. The error values distinguish an unknown group, an unsupported type, capacity limits, and invalid group information.

sections.title: Security and Management
sections.content:
A malicious PCEP speaker could create excessive or false associations, affect LSP operations, or reveal relationships between paths. The RFC RECOMMENDS securing the PCEP session with TLS. Indirect values can be used to avoid exposing sensitive business relationships.

Implementations MUST allow operator-configured associations and SHOULD allow configuration of their ID range. They SHOULD also let operators view associations that are configured or created dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: False associations could disrupt path handling or reveal which paths are related. The RFC recommends protecting PCEP with TLS and giving operators ways to configure and inspect groups.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Association ID
fields.desc: Identifies a group within its scope.

fields.name: IPv4 Association Source
fields.desc: Address that scopes the Association ID.
